title: The Anatomy of a Good Prompt — Check

questions.prompt: A colleague claims their prompts get better results because they say 'please' and end with 'thank you'. What's the most accurate response?
choices: They're correct — politeness measurably improves output quality across all models
Politeness is irrelevant to output quality; clarity and structural specificity are what move the needle
Politeness only helps with certain models, so they may be right depending on which one they're using
Politeness hurts output quality by wasting tokens, so they should stop
questions.explanation: Models have no preferences and don't reward courtesy. What changes output quality is unambiguous specification of context, task, constraints, examples, and output format. Politeness isn't harmful — it's just inert.

questions.prompt: You're drafting a follow-up email to a borrower who has gone quiet. Your first prompt produces an email that's the right tone but mentions a 'special discount' you never offered. What's the highest-leverage fix to the prompt?
choices: Add 'be more accurate' to the prompt and re-run
Add an explicit constraint: 'do not mention discounts, promotions, or any pricing terms not provided in this prompt'
Switch to a different AI tool, since this one is hallucinating
Re-run the same prompt several times and pick the response that doesn't mention a discount
questions.explanation: The avoid-list is one of the most under-used components of a good prompt. When the model invents something, telling it explicitly what not to do is faster and more reliable than re-rolling or adding vague accuracy instructions.

questions.prompt: Compare two prompts for the same task. Prompt A: 'Write a professional decline letter to a small business owner.' Prompt B (same plus): 'Recipient: 6-month-old retail shop, $9K monthly revenue, requested $50K. Length: under 120 words. Tone: warm, no marketing language. Avoid: any mention of competitors or future re-application. Output: email body only, no subject, no signature.' Which best characterizes the trade-off?
choices: Prompt A is better because it gives the model creative freedom; Prompt B over-constrains and produces mechanical output
Both prompts will produce roughly equivalent output because modern models infer the missing details
Prompt B is longer, which is the point — pinning down context, constraints, and output format dramatically narrows the response into a usable band
Prompt B is better for new users; experienced users should use shorter prompts like A
questions.explanation: The amateur instinct is to keep prompts short to give the model 'freedom.' The professional instinct is the opposite: more constraint produces more usable output. Longer, more specified prompts force the response into a narrower, much more shippable band.
